extracted.intended_audience: piano students, piano teachers, and aspiring professional pianists
extracted.subtask_description: Practical pedagogical guidance and evaluative criteria for developing piano technic, touch, interpretation, and practice routines. Focuses on hand position, finger action, artistic touch, practicing habits, and stylistic/interpretive aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of pianism
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear touch, intelligent phrasing, all varieties of tone, all the force the piano will stand, together with the greatest delicacy and the utmost speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are listed as the fundamental qualities that distinguish artists from ordinary students; acquire mastery over them as prerequisites for artistic playing. The text notes artists possess these as a matter of course while ordinary students often fail to produce sufficient clarity, force, tone variety, and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand position (arched hand)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arched hand position with rounded finger joints is the correct one; the finger-tips form a curve on the keys, knuckles somewhat elevated, and the middle finger often placed a little farther in on the key than the first and fifth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many authorities agree on this as the accepted position for passage playing. Quotes from Paderewski, Schelling, Goodson, Leginska, Leschetizky pupils, and others support securing a definite arched hand and firm finger joints; a few pianists use flatter fingers for specific cases (e.g., Tina Lerner) but the arched hand is the baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger action and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive finger movements and finger independence must be acquired in the beginning so they become second nature; raise fingers for passage work to ensure clarity and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach decided finger action in the early stages, then reduce visible motion as control becomes consummate. Leschetizky requires rigorous finger training (e.g., Czerny etudes) before higher work. Even artists who appear to have little motion acquired that control through early deliberate finger action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic touch (pressure and elastic/drawing-off)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop 'pressure' and 'elastic' or 'drawing-off' touches to obtain weight, crispness, and varied tone; 'feel how much the key resists you' and 'listen for the moment each sound begins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. William Mason favored pressure and elastic touches; Tobias Matthay's rules: feel the key's resistance and direct effort to the sound, not the key bed. The swifter the movement the louder; more gradual movement yields more beautiful tone. For brilliant tone one may 'hit the string by means of the key, but do not, by mistake, hit the key instead.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody hand vs technical (coloratura) hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Different hand position/condition is required for melody versus rapid passage work: the 'Melody Hand' uses outstretched, flat fingers with arm weight for full, caressing tone; the 'Technical/Coloratura Hand' uses well-arched, rounded fingers and active finger action for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use each hand-condition according to musical demand. Students should first acquire the coloratura (technical) hand to secure a clean reliable technic before attempting the flatter melody hand for lyrical tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice slowly and in sections (one difficulty at a time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practise slowly and in sections; work on one difficulty at a time, one hand at a time; do not at first practise the whole piece through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as 'Napoleon's tactics, one division at a time.' Slow practise lays a firm, rock-like basis for playing; if a player cannot control fingers slowly they cannot play fast. Avoid hurrying in fugue playing; dwell on measures until secure and then increase speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily technic routine: scales, arpeggios, octaves, chords, Bach
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain daily technical exercises—scales, arpeggios, octaves, chords, and Bach—selecting a few keys at a time rather than all keys every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists recommend regular technic practise (examples: Bachaus practises scales/arpeggios ~1/2 hour; some practise technic an hour/day). Practice these in various touches (legato often emphasized), dynamics, and articulations; overhaul technic weekly to keep it 'in running order.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and perfect a few etudes/studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Better to perfect a few etudes than to play at many; take one selection of Bach or an etude and polish it deeply (including transposing it in all keys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thuel Burnham and others advise perfecting and polishing a few technical pieces to the highest point possible rather than superficially playing many; this deepens technical command and musical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent exercises from repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: Create technical exercises out of the pieces being studied by reassigning hands, turning single notes into octaves, using more difficult fingering, changing rhythm, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to increase the difficulty so that when the passage is played as written it will seem easy. Also useful is transposition of repertoire through different keys to generalize technical command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technic maintenance ('pianist a mechanic')
rubrics_metrics.description: Technic is the mechanical part of music making and must be constantly tinkered with to keep it in running order; plan a daily schedule of exercises known to be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edwin Hughes compares technic upkeep to an engine driver maintaining a locomotive: regular, intentional maintenance prevents deterioration. Identify the exercises that benefit your playing and include them systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of arm weight, wrist and 'letting-go' principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ arm weight and appropriate wrist motion (e.g., wrist raised for black keys, depressed for white keys; use arm weight for ponderous or sonorous passages) and apply the 'letting-go' principle for freedom and dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chopin octave study needs wrist elevation/depression for black/white keys; Brahms and Schumann passages require arm weight and 'letting-go' for certain movements. Chords are to be played with pressure rather than percussion. Adjust wrist and arm use according to expressive and mechanical needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone idealization / spiritualization of tones
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not play bare printed tones; 'spiritualize' and idealize tones to reveal the composer's inner idea and the artist's insight behind the notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sherwood emphasizes getting 'behind the notes'—e.g., play the Chopin etude and Impromptu with a soft, velvety, limpid touch, making passages 'heavenly' or 'ethereal' where required. Interpretation demands finding and bringing out what is hidden behind the printed notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrasing, accentuation and ebb-and-flow shaping
rubrics_metrics.description: Shape phrases and measures with comparative accents and dynamic swellings (the 'ebb and flow' of measures), emphasizing appropriate beats and producing varied measure-to-measure dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sherwood's barcarolle instruction: 'Begin the first measure very softly, the second a trifle louder, the third louder still, the fourth falling off again.' Accent patterns (e.g., first beat slightly accented, second not) create musical undulation; use exaggeration of motion in the approach to keys to produce expressive shading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tempo confidence and risk-taking in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: While carefulness and accuracy are important, students must take risks and adopt appropriate tempos early rather than holding back through excessive caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Mason advised taking a risk from the beginning and sometimes suggested quicker tempi when appropriate. Overcautiousness can cost performance opportunities; controlled courage and tempo choices enhance musical expressiveness.
